Scaled‑dot‑product attention takes a query vector and a set of key–value pairs, computes the compatibility of the query with each key by a dot product, and then uses those scores to form a weighted sum of the corresponding values [S3].  
All dot products are first divided by √dₖ, where dₖ is the dimension of the queries and keys [S1].  
This scaling prevents the raw dot products from becoming excessively large when dₖ is big, which would push the subsequent soft‑max into regions with very small gradients [S1].  
By keeping the magnitude of the scores moderate, the soft‑max yields more stable attention weights and better learning dynamics [S1].

Multiple attention heads let the model attend to different representation subspaces simultaneously, whereas a single head would average these signals and lose diversity [S1]. By projecting queries, keys and values into several lower‑dimensional spaces and computing attention in parallel, each head can capture distinct patterns at different positions [S1]. The paper therefore uses eight parallel heads (h = 8), each with dimensions d_k = d_v = d_model / h = 64, yielding a total computational cost comparable to a single full‑dimensional head [S1].

The Transformer adds a positional encoding vector to each token embedding, where the encoding has the same dimension \(d_{\text{model}}\) and is defined by sine and cosine functions of varying frequencies: for even indices \(2i\) it uses \(\sin(\text{pos}/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}})\) and for odd indices \(2i+1\) it uses \(\cos(\text{pos}/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}})\) so that each dimension corresponds to a sinusoid whose wavelength forms a geometric progression [S1].  
These sinusoidal encodings were chosen because a fixed offset \(k\) between positions can be expressed as a linear function of the original encodings, making it easy for the model to learn relative positions [S1].  
The authors also tried learned positional embeddings and found that performance was nearly the same as with sinusoids [S2].  
However, they preferred the sinusoidal version because it can generalize to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training, whereas learned embeddings are limited to the lengths they were trained on [S1][S2].

Self‑attention layers have a per‑layer computational complexity of \(O(n^{2}\,d)\), require only a constant number of sequential operations \(O(1)\), and have a maximum path length of \(O(1)\) between any two positions [S2].  
Recurrent layers, in contrast, cost \(O(n\,d^{2})\) per layer, need \(O(n)\) sequential operations, and their maximum path length also scales as \(O(n)\) [S2].  
Thus, self‑attention is computationally more expensive than recurrent layers only when the sequence length \(n\) exceeds the representation dimension \(d\), but it offers far greater parallelism (constant‑time sequential depth) and a dramatically shorter longest dependency path [S1][S2].

Traditional spoken dialogue systems are built from separate components (voice activity detection, ASR, textual dialogue, TTS), which introduces a latency of several seconds between turns [S3]. Because they rely on text as an intermediate modality, important non‑linguistic cues such as emotion or non‑speech sounds are discarded, reducing the naturalness of the interaction [S3]. They also enforce strict speaker‑turn segmentation, preventing the handling of overlapping speech, interruptions, and interjections that occur in real conversations [S3]. These limitations together prevent pipelines from emulating the fluid, low‑latency experience of natural dialogue [S3].

Moshi’s architecture is built around three core components. The first component is Helium, a 7 B‑parameter text language model that supplies strong reasoning and linguistic knowledge to the system [S3][S2]. The second component is Mimi, a neural audio codec that combines semantic and acoustic information via residual vector quantization and knowledge distillation, enabling high‑quality, low‑bitrate audio tokenisation suitable for real‑time generation [S2][S3]. The third component is a streaming, hierarchical multi‑stream generation framework (the Depth Transformer) that simultaneously processes and produces semantic, acoustic, and, when using Inner Monologue, time‑aligned text tokens for both the user and Moshi, allowing full‑duplex spoken dialogue [S2][S3].

Moshi’s architecture is built around three core components: the Helium text language‑model backbone, the Mimi neural audio codec, and a streaming hierarchical multi‑stream generation architecture. Helium is a bespoke 7 B‑parameter text LLM that provides strong reasoning and linguistic knowledge to the system, enabling it to generate text tokens that guide speech output【S3】. Mimi is a neural audio codec that combines semantic and acoustic information using residual vector quantization and knowledge distillation, producing high‑quality audio tokens at low bitrates suitable for real‑time generation【S2】. The multi‑stream architecture streams hierarchical semantic and acoustic tokens for both the user and Moshi, and aligns text tokens (via Inner Monologue) with audio generation, allowing full‑duplex spoken dialogue without explicit turn‑taking【S2】. Inner Monologue further lets Moshi jointly model text and audio tokens, exploiting the text modality while remaining a speech‑to‑speech system【S1】. Together, these components enable Moshi to listen and speak simultaneously, generate expressive speech, and maintain low latency in real‑time conversation【S1】.

Moshi achieves full‑duplex capability by modeling two separate streams of semantic and acoustic tokens—one for the user and one for the system—within a single hierarchical Transformer architecture, so it can listen and speak simultaneously without a fixed turn‑taking boundary [S2][S3].  Its multi‑stream design, built on the Helium text LLM and the Mimi neural audio codec, allows the model to process the incoming user audio stream while concurrently generating its own output audio stream in real time [S3].  The Depth Transformer backbone supports streaming inference for both streams, enabling continuous, overlapping speech processing rather than sequential turn‑based interaction [S3].  Inner Monologue further integrates text and audio token generation, letting the system exploit text‑language knowledge while still operating as a pure speech‑to‑speech model, which reinforces the ability to handle simultaneous speaking and listening [S3].  By separating and hierarchically synchronizing these token streams, Moshi can manage overlapping utterances from both parties without explicit speaker‑turn modeling, achieving true full‑duplex dialogue [S2][S3].

Inner Monologue is a method in Moshi that generates text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens, enabling the model to decide whether to produce speech or transcription based on the relative delay between the two streams [S3]. By inserting a configurable delay between the text sequence (W_t) and the audio tokens (A_t,q), the language model can be made to let audio dictate the text (streaming ASR) or let text dictate the audio (streaming TTS) without changing the loss, architecture, or training data [S2][S1]. For streaming ASR, the text tokens are delayed (e.g., by 2 seconds) so the model listens to audio before generating text, and during inference the audio tokens are teacher‑forced while only text tokens are sampled, yielding word‑level alignments [S1][S2]. For streaming TTS, the audio tokens are delayed (e.g., by 2 seconds) giving the model look‑ahead on the text, and at inference the text tokens are teacher‑forced while only audio tokens are sampled, producing speech with low latency [S1][S2]. The same single hyper‑parameter for delay thus switches the system between a streaming ASR and a streaming TTS model, illustrating the flexibility of Inner Monologue [S1][S3].

The encoder network takes the raw input sequence and processes it at the fine‑grained (original) resolution before any down‑sampling occurs, while the decoder network receives the up‑sampled representations and operates again at the original resolution to reconstruct the output sequence [S2][S3].

H‑Net determines chunk boundaries with a learned routing module that examines the contextual embeddings of each byte and produces a binary indicator bₜ that marks where a chunk should end [S3].  During training the model discovers that spacelike bytes (e.g., whitespace) are strong semantic delimiters, so the single‑stage version places most cuts at those positions, mirroring the behavior of handcrafted SpaceByte tokenizers [S1].  In the two‑stage hierarchy, the first stage still favours spacelike bytes but also often cuts after the first few characters of a word, allowing the remaining characters to become highly predictable [S1].  Beyond these simple heuristics, H‑Net’s decisions are content‑aware: it frequently merges several words or punctuation marks when they form a coherent semantic unit, and it continues to place boundaries even when whitespace is removed, showing that the routing module uses broader context rather than fixed rules [S1].  The boundary indicators are then used by a down‑sampler to retain only the selected vectors, effectively compressing the byte stream according to the learned, data‑dependent segmentation [S3].

The ratio loss is introduced to prevent the model from collapsing to trivial extremes—either keeping almost every vector (which defeats the purpose of compression) or discarding too many vectors (which loses essential information)【S1】.  
It is inspired by load‑balancing losses used in Mixture‑of‑Experts models, and it provides a continuous supervisory signal that steers the network toward a desired compression level【S1】.  
In the loss formulation, **F** denotes the fraction of vectors that are actually selected (i.e., retained after chunking)【S1】.  
**G** is the average boundary probability output by the routing module, which serves as a differentiable proxy for the selection fraction【S1】.  
**N** is a hyper‑parameter that sets the target compression ratio, controlling how aggressively the model should down‑sample the sequence【S1】.

The ratio loss is added to prevent the model from collapsing to trivial solutions that either retain almost all vectors (undoing compression) or compress too aggressively and lose important information【S1】. It is inspired by load‑balancing losses used in Mixture‑of‑Experts models, providing a continuous supervisory signal that guides the network toward a desired compression ratio【S1】. In the loss formulation, F represents the fraction of vectors actually selected (i.e., retained after chunking)【S1】. G denotes the average boundary probability produced by the routing module, acting as a differentiable proxy for F that the optimizer can use【S1】. N is a hyper‑parameter that controls the target compression ratio, determining how aggressively the sequence should be down‑sampled【S1】. By training the model so that G approaches F and matches the target set by N, the ratio loss effectively steers the system toward the intended compression behavior【S1】.

Scaled dot‑product attention takes a query vector, compares it to each key vector by taking their dot product, and then uses those scores to form a weighted sum of the corresponding value vectors [S3][S1].  
The dot products are first divided by the square root of the key dimension \( \sqrt{d_k} \) before the softmax is applied [S1].  
This scaling prevents the raw dot‑product values from becoming too large when the dimension \(d_k\) is big, which would push the softmax into regions with very small gradients [S2].  
By keeping the magnitude of the scores moderate, the softmax yields more stable, informative attention weights [S2][S1].  
Thus the attention output is essentially a similarity‑weighted average of the values, with the scaling ensuring numerical stability.

Scaled‑dot‑product attention takes a query vector, computes its dot product with each key vector to measure similarity, scales those scores by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\), feeds them through a softmax to obtain a set of weights, and then returns a weighted sum of the corresponding value vectors [S1][S3]. The dot product gives a raw compatibility score between query and key, and the softmax turns these scores into a probability distribution that determines how much each value contributes to the output [S3]. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) is needed because, as the key dimension grows, the magnitude of the dot products tends to increase proportionally to \(\sqrt{d_k}\), which can push the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients [S2]. This scaling therefore keeps the softmax input in a range where it remains sensitive and numerically stable [S2].

Multi‑head attention is used because projecting queries, keys and values into several lower‑dimensional subspaces lets each head attend to different representation subspaces and positions, whereas a single head would average these signals and lose such diversity [S1]. The paper reports that a single‑head version performed 0.9 BLEU worse than the best multi‑head setting, confirming the benefit of multiple heads [S3]. In the Transformer they employ eight parallel attention heads [S1]. Each head uses dimensions d_k = d_v = d_model / h = 64, so that the total computational cost remains comparable to a single full‑dimensional head [S1]. This configuration (h = 8, d_k = d_v = 64) is the one used in the reported experiments [S1].

Inner Monologue is a modeling approach in Moshi that aligns text and audio tokens in a single hierarchical stream, decomposing speech on a per‑frame basis so that each prediction step emits a speech frame rather than waiting for an entire utterance [S4][S5]. By inserting a controllable delay between the two token types, the same Moshi model can be repurposed for either streaming text‑to‑speech or streaming speech‑to‑text [S2][S4]. For streaming TTS, the system delays the audio tokens (e.g., by 2 seconds) so that the model receives a short look‑ahead of text tokens before generating each audio frame, and inference is performed with teacher‑forced text tokens [S3]. For streaming ASR, the delay is applied to the text tokens (e.g., 2 seconds), allowing the model to listen to incoming audio before emitting text tokens, and inference uses teacher‑forced audio tokens [S3]. In both cases the delay creates a causal, low‑latency pipeline that yields real‑time generation with only a few hundred milliseconds of theoretical latency [S2]. This simple delay mechanism enables Moshi’s Inner Monologue to provide both streaming TTS and streaming ASR without changing the underlying architecture [S4][S5].
